messages.content: I want to develop domain-generalization methods that distinguish transferable predictive features from spurious features, without source-domain annotations or target-domain data. The goal is at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under unseen combinations of spurious correlations, while keeping average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM and preserving genuinely predictive features.

That sets two performance requirements alongside the central feature-selection challenge. The method should perform substantially better than ERM on the worst domain when spurious correlations appear in unseen combinations, but it should not gain that robustness by broadly discarding useful predictive information. The restrictions also matter: it cannot rely on source-domain annotations to identify environments or on target-domain data to tailor itself to the domains it will face.
What exactly is the distinction between a transferable predictive feature and a spurious one here?

A transferable predictive feature is useful for the prediction in a way that remains useful when the surrounding correlations change. A spurious feature can appear predictive in the available source data because of an incidental correlation, yet cease to be reliable under a different combination of correlations. The goal is to tell these apart well enough to generalize; it does not assume that every feature predictive in the sources is spurious, or that a feature can safely be removed merely because its reliability is uncertain.
So the method is not supposed to ignore everything that might vary across domains?

Right. Preserving genuinely predictive features is part of the goal, not an optional refinement. A method that suppresses useful information along with spurious cues could look robust in one respect while failing to retain the predictive signal the task calls for. The desired distinction is selective: resist misleading correlations without treating genuine predictiveness as something to eliminate.
How should I read the lack of source-domain annotations?

The method cannot be given annotations identifying which source domain an example belongs to. It therefore cannot make source-domain membership labels a prerequisite for distinguishing transferable from spurious features. That restriction is separate from the question of target-domain data: the method also cannot depend on having data from the target domains.
Does that mean ‘domain generalization’ here is just another name for fitting the source data well?

No. Fitting the source data is relevant because average source-domain accuracy must stay within one percentage point of ERM, but the distinguishing objective concerns performance when the spurious correlations are recombined in ways not seen before. High source accuracy by itself does not establish that the method has learned which features will transfer.
Why specify unseen combinations of spurious correlations rather than just saying ‘unseen domains’?

That wording makes the intended stress test more precise. The challenge is not merely that an evaluated domain has a new label or identity. It is that the correlations capable of misleading a predictor occur together in combinations the method has not encountered. A method that handles only familiar configurations would not address that stated condition.
Do the individual spurious correlations each have to be new, too?

The goal does not say that. Its explicit condition is *unseen combinations* of spurious correlations. We should not silently replace that with a different requirement that every individual correlation must itself be novel, or with the weaker requirement that only a domain name be novel.
And ‘worst-domain accuracy’ means the average across those domains?

No. Worst-domain accuracy concerns the least accurate domain in the evaluation being considered; it is not the average across domains. The required comparison is that this worst-domain accuracy be at least 5 percentage points higher than ERM’s under the unseen-combination condition. An improvement in an average that leaves the worst domain unimproved would not, by itself, meet that requirement.
Is that 5 percent relative to ERM, or 5 percentage points?

Five **percentage points**. It is an absolute difference between accuracy percentages, not a relative five-percent increase. The requirement is an improvement of at least that size in worst-domain accuracy compared with ERM.
There is also a one-percentage-point condition on source accuracy. Is that the same metric?

It is a different comparison. Average source-domain accuracy must remain within one percentage point of ERM’s average source-domain accuracy. Worst-domain accuracy addresses the most difficult domain under unseen combinations; average source-domain accuracy checks that the method stays close to ERM on the sources. Neither condition substitutes for the other.
Could strong worst-domain performance alone be enough if the method loses a lot of source accuracy?

Not under this goal. The requirements are joint: at least a 5-percentage-point worst-domain advantage over ERM under the stated condition, and average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM, while preserving genuinely predictive features. A large gain on one measure does not cancel a failure on another.
If average source accuracy stays close to ERM, does that prove genuinely predictive features were preserved?

Not necessarily. The average source-domain accuracy condition is a performance constraint, while preserving genuinely predictive features expresses what the method should retain. A close aggregate accuracy comparison alone does not tell us exactly which information a predictor is using. Both ideas matter, but they are not interchangeable.
What does the ERM comparison tell us, and what does it leave open?

ERM supplies the baseline for both numerical comparisons: the proposed method needs at least 5 percentage points more worst-domain accuracy under unseen combinations of spurious correlations, and its average source-domain accuracy must be within one percentage point of ERM. That comparison defines the target; it does not, on its own, specify an implementation or show that any method has already achieved it.
Would it be fair to say the challenge is partly about what information the method is allowed to use?

Yes. It must make a useful distinction between transferable and spurious predictive features without being handed source-domain annotations and without using target-domain data. Those are constraints on the method, not merely details of the accuracy measures. The method should generalize despite lacking those two sources of domain-specific guidance.
Could the evaluation still talk about a worst domain if the method has no source-domain annotations?

Yes; the training restriction and the performance measure play different roles. Saying the method has no source-domain annotations does not change what ‘worst-domain accuracy’ means as an evaluation criterion. Nor does evaluating performance on domains imply that target-domain data was available to the method for developing or adapting its predictions.
I want to avoid making the goal sound like we already know how to identify the good features. How would you phrase that uncertainty?

I would frame it as the problem to solve: develop methods that *can distinguish* transferable predictive features from spurious ones under those information restrictions. The feature distinction and the accuracy thresholds are objectives, not reported results. Nothing in the goal identifies a particular method or establishes that the distinction has already been achieved.
So the central tradeoff is not robustness versus prediction in general, but robustness without throwing away real signal?

Exactly. The aim is to resist spurious correlations when they appear in unseen combinations, while retaining genuinely predictive features and keeping average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. The ≥5-percentage-point worst-domain improvement and the source-accuracy constraint make both sides of that aim explicit.

For the domain-generalization goal, I want to propose CIFS: it adversarially partitions examples using cross-fitted ERM residuals into label-balanced pseudo-environments, penalizes feature drift, and distills ERM logits.

CIFS combines three ideas toward that goal. Cross-fitted ERM residuals inform an adversarial partition of the available examples into label-balanced pseudo-environments. A feature-drift penalty then discourages learned features from varying across those constructed environments, while distillation of ERM logits provides a way to retain predictive information from the ERM model. This is a proposed approach, not yet evidence that it meets the accuracy requirements.
What role do the pseudo-environments play if we do not have source-domain annotations?

They provide constructed groupings of examples where annotated source domains are unavailable. CIFS can use those groupings to examine feature drift without treating them as known, real domain identities. The proposal says how they are formed in broad terms—adversarially, using cross-fitted ERM residuals, with label balance—but does not claim that they recover the true domains.
Why use ERM residuals in making the partitions?

Residuals give a signal related to what ERM’s predictions do not account for well. Using them to guide the partition is intended to make the pseudo-environments informative for the robustness problem, rather than dividing examples without regard to ERM’s behavior. That is the rationale for the proposal; it is not a guarantee that the residuals isolate spurious features.
And what does ‘cross-fitted’ add to that description?

Conceptually, cross-fitting means obtaining residuals from ERM predictions made on examples outside the portion used to fit the corresponding predictor. That makes the residual signal less tied to how closely ERM can fit the very examples it trained on. The proposal does not specify a particular split scheme, number of fits, or residual formula.
Is the adversarial partition meant to find the actual source domains?

Not necessarily. Its stated output is *pseudo-environments*: partitions constructed for the method’s purposes, rather than supplied source-domain annotations or a claim of recovered domain labels. ‘Adversarially’ indicates that the partition is sought in a challenging way using the cross-fitted ERM residuals; the precise adversarial objective is not specified here.
Why require those pseudo-environments to be label-balanced?

Label balance prevents the constructed groups from being distinguished merely by an uncontrolled difference in their label composition. That helps keep the comparison focused on differences other than a simple shift in labels. The proposal does not specify an exact balancing rule or say that balance alone makes the pseudo-environments representative of unseen domains.
Could a residual-driven partition still reflect something genuinely predictive rather than a spurious correlation?

Yes. A residual is not, by itself, a certificate that a feature is spurious. CIFS proposes to use residual-informed pseudo-environments and a feature-drift penalty to pursue the distinction, while ERM-logit distillation is part of its attempt to retain useful predictive behavior. Whether the combination actually separates transferable signal from spurious signal remains a question for evaluation.
What exactly is penalized when you say ‘feature drift’?

The proposal names a penalty on feature drift, meaning it discourages changes in the learned features across the constructed pseudo-environments. It does not define a specific drift measure, representation layer, or penalty formula. Those details should not be treated as settled just from the phrase ‘penalizes feature drift.’
Why would discouraging drift help with domain generalization?

The intended connection is that features that behave consistently across challenging pseudo-environments may be better candidates for transfer than features whose behavior shifts with the constructed partition. But consistency across these particular pseudo-environments is only a useful design intuition, not proof of transfer to every unseen combination of spurious correlations.
Could a feature-drift penalty also suppress a feature we actually need?

That is a relevant risk. A genuinely predictive feature should be preserved under the original goal, and penalizing drift too indiscriminately could conflict with that. CIFS pairs the penalty with distillation of ERM logits, but the proposal alone does not establish that this pairing prevents the loss of genuinely predictive features.
What are ERM logits contributing that residuals are not?

They have different roles. Cross-fitted ERM residuals guide the adversarial construction of label-balanced pseudo-environments. ERM logits are the outputs CIFS proposes to distill, providing a predictive reference from ERM. The former helps define where to look for potentially problematic variation; the latter is intended to help retain ERM’s predictive information while feature drift is penalized.
Does distilling logits mean CIFS is required to reproduce every ERM prediction?

No such requirement is stated. ‘Distills ERM logits’ says that ERM’s logits inform learning; it does not specify exact agreement, a distillation loss, or how distillation is balanced against the feature-drift penalty. Reproducing every ERM output exactly would be a stronger claim than the proposal makes.
How does this address the restriction on target-domain data?

CIFS constructs pseudo-environments from the available examples using cross-fitted ERM residuals, rather than requiring target-domain data to define them. That makes the proposal compatible in concept with the no-target-data goal. It does not imply that the constructed partitions will match the target domains or reveal their future spurious-correlation combinations.
Would it be accurate to say CIFS has already met the ≥5-percentage-point worst-domain target?

No. CIFS is a proposal for addressing the goal, not a reported result. The relevant requirement remains at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under unseen combinations of spurious correlations. The description of CIFS supplies no measured worst-domain accuracy.
The other requirement is average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. Is that what the logit distillation is for?

Preserving ERM’s predictive information through logit distillation is consistent with that aim, as well as with preserving genuinely predictive features. But distillation by itself does not establish that CIFS will keep average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. That threshold remains a condition the proposed method would need to satisfy.
Can we describe the three parts without implying a particular training schedule?

Yes: CIFS uses cross-fitted ERM residuals to adversarially partition examples into label-balanced pseudo-environments, penalizes feature drift, and distills ERM logits. That identifies the proposed components and their roles without asserting a particular order of optimization steps, number of iterations, or implementation of any loss.
Are label-balanced pseudo-environments interchangeable with source domains for measuring worst-domain accuracy?

No. They are constructed groupings used by CIFS, not necessarily the domains on which worst-domain accuracy is assessed. The evaluation requirement concerns worst-domain accuracy under unseen combinations of spurious correlations relative to ERM. Success on the constructed pseudo-environments alone would not automatically demonstrate the required improvement on that evaluation.
Then the cautious claim is that CIFS tries to expose unstable features without sacrificing the useful ones?

Yes, with its specific mechanism kept visible: residual-informed, adversarial, label-balanced pseudo-environments provide the comparisons; penalizing feature drift pushes against variation across them; and ERM-logit distillation supplies a counterweight aimed at retaining predictive information. Whether that achieves the desired distinction and satisfies both numerical comparisons remains open in the proposal.
One more nuance: does using ERM both for residuals and for logits make ERM the final answer rather than a baseline?

No. ERM has two roles within the proposal—its cross-fitted residuals inform the partitions, and its logits are distilled—and it remains the comparison baseline for the goal. CIFS is proposed as a distinct method intended to improve worst-domain accuracy without losing much average source-domain accuracy. Those uses of ERM do not imply that CIFS must simply behave identically to it.
Can CIFS’s residual-based pseudo-environments expose coupled color–texture shortcuts without penalizing predictive shape features?

That is the key uncertainty for this proposal. Residual-based partitions might reveal differences associated with a color–texture shortcut, but residuals do not identify *why* ERM made an error. And a feature-drift penalty applied across the resulting pseudo-environments might affect predictive shape features too. CIFS’s components make the distinction possible to pursue; they do not establish that it succeeds.
What makes a coupled color–texture shortcut harder to expose than a single shortcut?

Color and texture could act together as a predictive cue, so looking for variation in either one alone may not reveal the behavior of the combination. The question is whether the pseudo-environments expose that joint reliance. Nothing in the proposal guarantees that an adversarial partition guided by ERM residuals will separate examples in the particular way needed to make it visible.
Could the residuals reveal the shortcut even if they do not name color or texture?

Potentially. Residuals reflect discrepancies in ERM’s predictions, not semantic labels for the features involved. If reliance on the coupled cue contributes to those discrepancies, a residual-informed partition could help expose a difference worth penalizing. But the same residual pattern could have another explanation, and the proposal does not establish which explanation applies.
Does cross-fitting settle that ambiguity?

No. Cross-fitting helps keep the residuals from being merely a reflection of predictions on the exact examples used to fit the corresponding ERM predictor. It does not turn residuals into a direct test of whether color and texture are spurious, or whether shape is genuinely predictive.
What if ERM follows the color–texture shortcut and still makes accurate predictions on the available examples?

Then residuals might offer little indication of that reliance. A shortcut can be a generalization concern even when it works well on available examples. That possibility is one reason the question cannot be answered simply by pointing to residual-based partitions.
And if the partition does reveal something, is the feature-drift penalty necessarily aimed at color and texture?

Not necessarily. The penalty discourages feature drift across the constructed pseudo-environments; it does not come with an intrinsic label saying ‘penalize the color–texture shortcut, but spare shape.’ Whether it targets the unwanted dependence rather than useful shape information depends on what differences those pseudo-environments actually expose and how the learned features respond.
Why might a predictive shape feature appear to drift across pseudo-environments?

The constructed groups are based on residuals, not on a guarantee that only shortcut-related properties differ between them. If a useful shape feature varies across those groups, a drift penalty could put pressure on it as well. Its being predictive does not, by itself, make it invariant to every grouping the method constructs.
Does making the pseudo-environments label-balanced protect shape?

Label balance limits one simple source of differences between groups: their label composition. It does not ensure that shape features have the same behavior across groups, nor that any remaining difference is caused by a color–texture shortcut. So it helps define a more focused comparison, but it is not a safeguard that selectively preserves shape.
Could ERM-logit distillation provide that safeguard instead?

It could provide pressure to retain predictive information represented in ERM’s outputs, which is relevant to preserving shape if ERM uses it. But the logits do not distinguish shape-based predictions from shortcut-based ones. Distillation therefore cannot, on its own, certify that shape is retained while the coupled color–texture dependence is removed.
So distillation might preserve some of the shortcut as well?

That is possible in principle. If ERM’s logits reflect reliance on color and texture, distilling them could also carry some of that behavior forward. The proposal combines distillation with a feature-drift penalty; the open question is whether those pressures can retain genuinely predictive shape information while reducing shortcut reliance, rather than preserving or suppressing both indiscriminately.
Is ‘expose’ a weaker claim than ‘eliminate’ in my question?

Yes. Exposing the shortcut would mean the pseudo-environments make its influence discernible or consequential for learning. Eliminating it would be a further claim about the resulting predictor. Your question also asks whether shape avoids being penalized, which is distinct from whether the shortcut becomes visible in the first place.
Can the two parts of the question have different answers?

They can. The pseudo-environments might expose a coupled color–texture dependence while the drift penalty still affects predictive shape. Conversely, shape might be retained without the partition adequately exposing the coupled shortcut. The desired outcome requires both: make the shortcut apparent to the method and avoid treating useful shape information as something to suppress.
Would observing different residuals across the pseudo-environments prove that the color–texture coupling was found?

No. A difference in residuals would show that the constructed groups differ with respect to ERM’s prediction discrepancies. Because residuals do not specify the responsible features, that observation alone would not identify a coupled color–texture shortcut or show that predictive shape features were spared.
How should I state the question without assuming shape always is predictive?

The wording ‘predictive shape features’ already makes the condition explicit: it asks about shape features that genuinely help prediction, not every feature describable as shape. You can ask whether CIFS exposes coupled color–texture shortcuts *while preserving genuinely predictive shape features*. That keeps the potential conflict clear without declaring all shape information useful.
What would be the most careful answer to the original question at this stage?

CIFS might do so, but its stated mechanism does not yet establish it. Cross-fitted ERM residuals can guide adversarial, label-balanced pseudo-environments without identifying the features behind the residuals. Penalizing drift across those groups could challenge coupled color–texture reliance, but could also penalize predictive shape features; ERM-logit distillation may help retain useful predictions without guaranteeing that separation. Whether CIFS achieves both parts of the question remains open.

Here is the hypothesis I want to test: on ShapeColorTexture-8 unseen color–texture combinations, CIFS beats ERM by at least 5 percentage points in worst-domain accuracy, while losing no more than 1 percentage point in source accuracy and shape-probe accuracy.

That makes the earlier question testable without treating its answer as known. The hypothesis predicts a ≥5-percentage-point worst-domain advantage over ERM on the unseen color–texture combinations in ShapeColorTexture-8, alongside losses of ≤1 percentage point in each of source accuracy and shape-probe accuracy. Those are predicted outcomes, not observed results.
Does the worst-domain part specifically address the coupled color–texture concern?

It targets that concern by asking whether CIFS holds up on unseen *combinations* of color and texture, rather than merely retaining accuracy where their relationship is familiar. A worst-domain improvement there would be consistent with reduced reliance on a brittle coupled shortcut. The accuracy comparison alone would not identify exactly which features produced the improvement.
Why use worst-domain accuracy instead of reporting only one overall accuracy?

Worst-domain accuracy focuses the comparison on the domain where performance is lowest. If CIFS improves an overall average while still struggling badly on one of the unseen combinations, that would not satisfy the ≥5-percentage-point worst-domain prediction. The hypothesis asks for a gain at the difficult end, not just a gain after averaging.
Is the five-point threshold a relative five-percent gain?

No. It is at least **5 percentage points** in accuracy compared with ERM’s worst-domain accuracy under the stated condition. Percentage points describe the difference between two accuracy percentages; they are not a relative percentage increase.
What work is the source-accuracy condition doing here?

It limits how much performance CIFS may give up on the source data while pursuing the worst-domain gain. The hypothesis is not simply that CIFS can improve robustness at any cost: its source accuracy is predicted to be no more than 1 percentage point below ERM’s. That condition does not, by itself, establish why the model performs as it does.
And why include a shape-probe condition separately?

It speaks directly to the concern about penalizing predictive shape features. The hypothesis predicts that CIFS loses no more than 1 percentage point of shape-probe accuracy relative to ERM, in addition to staying close in source accuracy. Source accuracy alone might not reveal a loss on that probe, so the two conditions express different aspects of the proposed tradeoff.
Does a one-point shape-probe loss prove that shape features have been preserved?

Not conclusively. It would meet the hypothesis’s stated shape-probe accuracy condition, but a probe score is a performance observation, not a complete account of every feature the predictor uses. The careful claim is that the hypothesis constrains the measured loss on the shape probe to ≤1 percentage point; it does not promise a full causal explanation of the learned representation.
Could source accuracy be close to ERM while shape-probe accuracy drops more than a point?

Yes, conceptually, and that is why the hypothesis states both limits. Staying within 1 percentage point on source accuracy would not compensate for losing more than 1 percentage point on shape-probe accuracy. Both predicted limits would need to hold, as well as the worst-domain improvement, for the complete hypothesis to hold.
What if shape-probe accuracy stays close but the worst-domain gain is less than five points?

Then the shape-probe prediction could hold, but the complete hypothesis would not: it specifically predicts a worst-domain improvement of at least 5 percentage points over ERM on the unseen color–texture combinations. Preserving probe accuracy is not a substitute for that improvement.
Is ‘beats ERM’ meant to apply to all three accuracy measures?

Not in the same way. The hypothesis predicts that CIFS **exceeds** ERM by ≥5 percentage points in worst-domain accuracy. For source and shape-probe accuracy, it allows CIFS to be lower, but by no more than 1 percentage point on each. It does not require CIFS to outperform ERM on either of those latter measures.
Should I say ‘at most one point total’ across source and shape-probe accuracy?

No. The wording gives a ≤1-percentage-point loss in source accuracy **and** a ≤1-percentage-point loss in shape-probe accuracy. Combining them into a single total-loss allowance would change the stated condition.
Does the hypothesis assert that the pseudo-environments actually isolate color and texture?

No. It predicts an outcome for CIFS on ShapeColorTexture-8; it does not claim that its residual-based pseudo-environments perfectly identify the color–texture shortcut. If the prediction holds, the result would bear on the practical question raised earlier, but the hypothesis itself does not settle the internal mechanism.
Could the hypothesis hold even if our explanation of why CIFS works is incomplete?

Yes. The stated prediction is about relative accuracies under a specified condition. Meeting those thresholds would not, by itself, establish that residual-based partitioning exposed exactly the coupled shortcut or that the feature-drift penalty acted only on it. The performance claim and the proposed explanation should remain distinct.
Does the name ShapeColorTexture-8 tell us how many unseen combinations are involved?

The hypothesis names ShapeColorTexture-8 and specifies unseen color–texture combinations, but it does not state how many combinations are in the evaluation. It would be unwarranted to infer a count, a partitioning scheme, or other dataset details from the name alone.
Is this a hypothesis about every possible shift involving color and texture?

No. Its scope is the unseen color–texture combinations in ShapeColorTexture-8. The broader domain-generalization goal motivates it, but this prediction should not be stretched into a claim about every possible shift or every dataset.
I also do not want to imply that shape-probe accuracy measures source accuracy again.

Keeping the measures named separately does that: source accuracy is one condition, and shape-probe accuracy is another. Both have a maximum predicted loss of 1 percentage point relative to ERM, but they address different questions. The hypothesis does not specify the shape probe’s construction, so it is best not to add an unstated definition of its data or procedure.
Can you restate the hypothesis in one sentence without making it sound like a result?

We hypothesize that, on ShapeColorTexture-8 unseen color–texture combinations, CIFS will exceed ERM’s worst-domain accuracy by at least 5 percentage points while losing no more than 1 percentage point relative to ERM in either source accuracy or shape-probe accuracy.
What is the distinction between that prediction and answering whether CIFS avoids penalizing predictive shape features?

The prediction makes the concern observable through the shape-probe accuracy limit, while pairing it with the required worst-domain gain. Avoiding a substantial probe-accuracy loss would support the narrower performance claim made here; it would not automatically show that no predictive shape feature was penalized at all. The question about the precise feature-level behavior remains more specific than these three accuracy comparisons.

To test the CIFS question, I plan to generate ShapeColorTexture-8 splits, train CIFS and ERM without domain labels, and compare their unseen-combination worst-domain, source, and shape-probe accuracy.

That plan connects the feature-level concern to three performance comparisons. The ShapeColorTexture-8 splits provide the setting, CIFS and ERM are trained without domain labels, and the comparison asks both whether CIFS improves the difficult unseen color–texture combinations and whether it retains source and shape-probe accuracy. These are planned steps, not results.
Why is it important to say explicitly that both CIFS and ERM are trained without domain labels?

It keeps the comparison aligned with the constraint that the method should not rely on source-domain annotations. It also makes clear that domain labels are not an input granted to one training procedure but withheld from the other. The plan does not specify any further training details.
But how can we compare worst-domain accuracy if training uses no domain labels?

Training inputs and evaluation groupings serve different purposes. The plan rules out domain labels for training CIFS and ERM; reporting worst-domain accuracy requires assessing performance by domain in the comparison. Using a domain distinction to report an evaluation metric does not, by itself, mean either model was trained with domain labels.
Should the unseen-combination comparison be treated as part of source accuracy?

No. The plan names unseen-combination worst-domain accuracy and source accuracy as separate comparisons. Keeping them separate matters: source performance indicates what is retained on the source side, while worst-domain performance on unseen combinations addresses the proposed generalization challenge.
Where does shape-probe accuracy fit into the plan?

It is the third named accuracy comparison. It bears on the concern that discouraging feature drift might also harm predictive shape information. The plan calls for comparing CIFS and ERM on shape-probe accuracy, but does not specify how the probe is built or administered.
Does comparing shape-probe accuracy directly show which features CIFS penalized?

Not directly. It measures performance on the named probe; it does not provide a complete account of which features were penalized or why. Alongside the other two accuracies, it helps assess the practical concern in the question without making the metric into a feature-level explanation.
What is the purpose of generating ShapeColorTexture-8 splits before training?

The splits establish the setting in which the planned training and comparisons will take place, including the unseen-combination comparison. The plan does not give the splits’ sizes, the number of combinations, or a procedure for generating them, so those particulars remain unspecified.
Should we assume the name ShapeColorTexture-8 fixes those details?

No. The name identifies the setting, but the plan itself does not spell out its split construction or other dataset particulars. We can accurately say that ShapeColorTexture-8 splits will be generated without inferring additional specifications from the name.
What exactly makes this a comparison rather than just an evaluation of CIFS?

ERM is trained as well, without domain labels, and both methods’ accuracies are compared on the three named measures. That gives CIFS a reference for unseen-combination worst-domain, source, and shape-probe accuracy rather than interpreting its scores in isolation.
If CIFS looks better on source accuracy, does the plan let us skip the worst-domain comparison?

No. The planned comparison includes all three measures. A source-accuracy difference alone would not answer whether CIFS handles unseen color–texture combinations in the worst domain, and it would not replace the shape-probe comparison either.
And could a worst-domain comparison alone settle the question about predictive shape?

No. That comparison addresses performance under unseen combinations, but the question also asks whether predictive shape features are penalized. The separate shape-probe accuracy comparison is included to examine that concern, with the caveat that probe accuracy is not a complete feature-level account.
Does this plan require us to feed target-domain data into CIFS?

It does not call for that. The planned training is without domain labels, and the unseen-combination accuracies are named as comparison outcomes, not as data for tailoring CIFS during training. The distinction between training and evaluation should remain clear.
Are CIFS’s pseudo-environments the same thing as the domains used for worst-domain accuracy?

The plan does not equate them. CIFS’s residual-based pseudo-environments are constructed for its proposed learning approach; worst-domain accuracy is an evaluation comparison on the unseen combinations. Treating those constructed groups as if they were automatically the evaluation domains would add a claim the plan does not make.
Do we need to specify a particular implementation of the feature-drift penalty in this plan?

Not to state this plan faithfully. The plan says to train CIFS and ERM without domain labels and compare the three accuracies; it does not specify a drift metric, penalty formula, or other implementation choices. Those should not be presented as already decided.
What about the ERM residuals and logits—are they still part of what ‘train CIFS’ means here?

They identify the previously proposed CIFS approach: residual-informed pseudo-environments, a feature-drift penalty, and ERM-logit distillation. This plan does not add a training schedule or new rules for those components. Its emphasis is on generating the splits, training both methods without domain labels, and making the stated accuracy comparisons.
Could we claim the plan tests whether the pseudo-environments expose the coupled color–texture shortcut?

It tests the question through outcomes that bear on it: worst-domain accuracy on unseen combinations, together with source and shape-probe accuracy. Those comparisons can assess whether CIFS delivers the intended performance pattern. On their own, they would not prove that the pseudo-environments exposed a particular shortcut internally.
So the wording should avoid saying the planned comparison will establish the mechanism?

Yes. ‘Compare’ is appropriately cautious. It commits the plan to examining the named accuracies for CIFS and ERM, not to a predetermined result or a definitive explanation of how any difference arises.
Can I describe the plan in one sentence without adding any unstated split or probe details?
Generate ShapeColorTexture-8 splits, train CIFS and ERM without domain labels, and compare their worst-domain accuracy on unseen color–texture combinations, source accuracy, and shape-probe accuracy.
If those comparisons disagree with one another, is that still within the scope of the plan?

Yes. The plan is to compare three distinct measures, not to assume they will move together. Differences among them would matter for interpreting the proposed tradeoff, but the plan does not predict an observed outcome or resolve it in advance.
What should we be careful not to imply when introducing the experiment?

Avoid implying that the splits have already been generated, the models have already been trained, or any accuracy has been measured. Also avoid treating the evaluation domains as training annotations or the shape-probe comparison as proof of precisely which features CIFS uses. The stated next steps are the split generation, label-free training of CIFS and ERM, and comparison of the three named accuracies.
Let's run five-seed ShapeColorTexture-8 trials comparing CIFS with ERM, without domain labels or target access, and measure held-out worst-domain, source, and shape-probe accuracies.

That specifies the activity: run the CIFS–ERM comparison across five seeds under the no-domain-label and no-target-access restrictions, then measure all three named accuracies. It does not yet report any results.
What does the five-seed part add to the comparison?

It calls for five runs associated with different seeds, rather than relying on a single run. That gives the comparison a way to reflect variation across runs. The activity does not specify the seed values or how the resulting measurements will be summarized.
Should I treat five seeds as five different held-out domains?

No. Seeds distinguish runs; domains distinguish evaluation groupings. The activity specifies five-seed trials and a held-out worst-domain accuracy measurement, but it does not equate a seed with a domain or state how many held-out domains there are.
Does ‘without domain labels’ apply only to CIFS?

Because prediction on source examples alone can reflect either useful label information or an incidental correlation. FACTOR-Guard proposes cue-ablation tests to examine whether shape or texture is essential for predicting the label before deciding what can be swapped. Whether that examination is sufficient to identify transferable rather than spurious information is an open performance question, not something the proposal resolves by definition.
Could both shape and texture be protected?

The description allows protection of label-essential shape or texture; it does not state that only one may qualify. Nor does it say that either must qualify in every setting. The protection decision is meant to depend on what the proposed tests indicate about label-essential information.
Does ‘swaps only unprotected factors’ specify which factors are swapped in every example?

No. It sets a boundary on eligibility: protected factors are not to be swapped. It does not specify how eligible factors are chosen for any particular example, how many swaps occur, or the mechanics of a swap.
Does source-only training mean the method can look at target examples as long as they have no labels?

No. ‘Source-only’ rules out using target examples for training, labeled or unlabeled. It keeps the proposal aligned with the goal of developing a method without target-domain data. The description does not give a more detailed data-access protocol.
What about source-domain annotations?

The broader goal calls for methods that work without source-domain annotations. FACTOR-Guard is proposed in that context, using cross-fitted cue-ablation tests and source-only swaps rather than identifying a need for supplied domain identities. The proposal does not spell out an implementation, so it should not be treated as proof that every possible implementation respects the no-domain-annotation restriction.
Why make the swaps conditional on the ablation tests instead of swapping every cue?

The proposed reason is preservation: unrestricted swapping could interfere with shape or texture that genuinely helps determine the label. By protecting cues judged label-essential, FACTOR-Guard aims to challenge other factors without automatically treating all variable information as disposable. That is its design intent, not a demonstrated guarantee.
How does that connect to the worst-domain objective?

Swapping unprotected factors is intended to reduce dependence on cues that may fail when spurious correlations occur in unseen combinations. To meet the broader objective, a method would need at least 5 percentage points higher worst-domain accuracy than ERM under those combinations. FACTOR-Guard’s proposal supplies a possible mechanism for pursuing that objective, but no worst-domain score is stated for it.
And the source-accuracy requirement?

Protecting label-essential shape or texture is intended to retain useful predictive information while swaps challenge other factors. The broader requirement is to keep average source-domain accuracy within one percentage point of ERM. The proposal does not report source accuracy or establish that its protection decisions will satisfy that limit.
Could we say that protecting label-essential texture is especially important when texture defines class?

Yes, as a conceptual reading of the proposal. When texture is needed for class identity, treating it indiscriminately as a cue to swap would conflict with preserving genuinely predictive features. FACTOR-Guard proposes to protect texture when its cross-fitted cue-ablation tests identify it as label-essential; that remains a proposed safeguard rather than a verified outcome in every texture-dependent setting.
Is FACTOR-Guard just a new name for swapping color and texture?

No. Its defining rule is conditional protection: test whether shape or texture is label-essential, protect those cues, and swap only factors left unprotected. The proposal does not say that color or texture must always be swapped, or give a fixed list of factors to swap in every setting.
Can the proposal specify its logic without claiming the tests always get it right?

Yes: FACTOR-Guard uses cross-fitted cue-ablation tests to decide which label-essential shape or texture information to protect, then confines source-only swaps to unprotected factors. That expresses the proposed decision rule while leaving open whether the tests reliably identify essential information and whether the resulting method achieves the domain-generalization targets.
What is the shortest careful description of FACTOR-Guard?

FACTOR-Guard proposes cross-fitted cue-ablation tests to protect label-essential shape or texture and swaps only unprotected factors during source-only training; its effectiveness remains to be established.
Can FACTOR-Guard protect label-essential texture without mistakenly protecting correlated color when both predict source labels?

That remains an open question. FACTOR-Guard proposes cross-fitted cue-ablation tests to decide what to protect, but when texture and color both predict source labels, their separate contributions may be hard to distinguish. The intended outcome is to protect texture because it is label-essential without protecting color merely because it accompanies texture in the sources. The proposal does not establish that its tests can always make that distinction.
Why isn’t source-label prediction enough to decide which cue to protect?

Both cues can predict source labels even if they play different roles. In the situation you describe, texture is essential to the class distinction, whereas color might be predictive only through its correlation with texture. Source predictive accuracy alone does not tell us which of those explanations accounts for a cue’s apparent usefulness.
Wouldn’t removing texture in an ablation test make its importance obvious?

Not necessarily. If color remains available and predicts much the same source labels, the predictor might still perform well without texture. That could make texture look less important in a test, even though texture carries the label-essential distinction. The possibility illustrates why correlated cues complicate ablation-based protection; it does not say that FACTOR-Guard necessarily makes that mistake.
Could the opposite mistake happen when color is ablated?

Yes, depending on what the test measures and how the predictor responds. A change in performance after removing color would not automatically mean color is essential to class identity. It could reflect how the predictor used the correlation in source examples. The proposal does not specify a rule that resolves every such ambiguity.
So when I say ‘mistakenly protecting correlated color,’ what is the mistake exactly?

The mistake would be treating color as label-essential solely because it predicts source labels alongside texture, when its predictive value comes from their correlation rather than from a necessary class distinction. That is different from saying color can never be useful. The question asks whether FACTOR-Guard can avoid conflating these two kinds of usefulness in this situation.
Does ‘label-essential texture’ mean texture must be the only useful feature?

No. It means texture carries information needed for the label distinction at issue. Other features might also be predictive, but their predictive value in the sources does not automatically make them essential. The question contrasts a stipulated essential cue with a correlated cue that could be protected for the wrong reason.
What does cross-fitting contribute if the cues are correlated?

Cross-fitting can make an ablation assessment less dependent on predictions made on the same examples used to fit the corresponding predictor. It does not, by itself, break the correlation between color and texture or identify which cue defines the label. It addresses one concern about assessing predictions, not every ambiguity about what makes a cue essential.
Could both cues pass a test that looks for a loss of accuracy after ablation?

Conceptually, they could, because a test’s response can depend on how the predictor uses both cues. But FACTOR-Guard’s description does not specify the exact ablation test or its protection criterion, so we cannot assert that this will happen or assign either cue a test outcome. The question is whether the proposed tests distinguish essential texture from correlated color, not whether both necessarily pass.
Could neither cue appear essential if each can stand in for the other in the sources?

That is another conceptual risk. If removing either cue separately leaves a correlated substitute, separate ablations might understate the importance of the information carried by texture. Whether that occurs for FACTOR-Guard depends on details and behavior not given here. It shows why protecting essential texture cannot simply be assumed from the word ‘ablation.’
Is the challenge about identifying a shortcut, or about protecting a real signal?

Both sides matter. FACTOR-Guard needs to avoid treating correlated color as label-essential merely because it predicts source labels, while protecting texture when texture really is needed for class identity. Avoiding one error without avoiding the other would not fully answer your question.
If FACTOR-Guard protects both texture and color, has it at least done the important part?

And if it leaves both unprotected?

Could protecting color ever be the correct choice?

In principle, yes, if color were itself label-essential in the setting being considered. Your question is more specific: color predicts source labels alongside label-essential texture, and you are worried it may be protected *merely because it is correlated*. We should not generalize from that concern to a rule that color is always spurious.
Is there a difference between color being correlated with texture and color being correlated with the label?

Yes. If texture helps determine the label and color accompanies texture in the sources, color can also predict source labels without necessarily carrying the label-essential information. The distinction matters because a source-label association is an observation about prediction, while essentiality is the property FACTOR-Guard is trying to use for protection.
Does the lack of domain labels make this question harder?

Whether that information suffices to tell essential texture from correlated color is exactly the uncertainty your question raises.
Would source-only training necessarily reveal that color is just correlated?

Can we infer the answer from the name FACTOR-Guard?

No. The name and design express an intent to guard label-essential factors. They do not certify that cross-fitted cue-ablation tests correctly identify essential texture or decline to protect correlated color when the two are jointly predictive in the sources.
Would a good source-accuracy result answer the question?

Not on its own. A predictor could score well on source examples using either texture, correlated color, or both. Source accuracy therefore would not, by itself, tell us which cue FACTOR-Guard designated as protected or whether that designation matched the distinction in your question.
What if I only check whether texture remains useful to the final predictor?

That would address part of the concern, but not whether color was mistakenly protected. Your question is about the *selectivity* of FACTOR-Guard’s protection: retaining label-essential texture while not giving the same protected status to color solely on the strength of its source-label correlation.
Is protecting a cue the same as proving the final model uses it?

No. Protection is a proposed rule about which factors are exempt from swapping during training. Whether the final predictor uses texture, and in what way, is a separate question. Likewise, not protecting color does not itself prove that the final predictor never uses color.
So what is the careful way to state this as an unresolved issue?

The unresolved issue is whether FACTOR-Guard’s cross-fitted cue-ablation tests can distinguish texture that is essential to the label from color that predicts source labels because it is correlated with texture, so that it protects the former without mistakenly protecting the latter. The proposal defines that intended distinction, but does not establish that it can reliably make it.
